variants.title: Climb the evidence ladder
variants.context: The evidence ladder runs from signal to slice to trace: validate the signal, compare bounded slices, inspect representative traces, reproduce the behavior, then record the attribution. A fleet average says something moved; the slice and the trace say where and how.
variants.prompt: Cost per successful task rises 40 percent overnight. Put the investigation in order.

items.text: Inspect representative traces: put an expensive trace beside a healthy peer and find the first divergent span or version.
Compare bounded slices: break the increase down by feature, route, tenant class, language, intent, and prompt version.
Reproduce the behavior: replay with preserved inputs and controlled dependencies where policy and privacy allow it.
Validate the signal: confirm the cost event definition, the successful-task denominator, missing data, duplicates, sampling, and the deployment window.
Record the attribution: link the alert, the trace, the changed component, the decision, and the new regression case.

variants.hint: Before you explain a movement, check that the movement is real.
variants.explanation: A cost increase can be traffic, larger prompts, a route change, lower cache reuse, or repeated failures, so the denominator is validated before any slice is blamed.

variants.title: Climb the evidence ladder
variants.context: The evidence ladder runs from signal to slice to trace: validate the signal, compare bounded slices, inspect representative traces, reproduce the behavior, then record the attribution. A fleet average says something moved; the slice and the trace say where and how.
variants.prompt: Sampled groundedness falls in one language while the fleet score barely moves. Put the investigation in order.

items.text: Compare bounded slices: separate language, retrieval corpus version, tenant class, and risk tier instead of trusting the fleet average.
Record the attribution: file the corpus change, the trace, and the decision as one linked regression case.
Inspect representative traces: put an ungrounded answer beside a grounded peer and locate the first differing retrieval or prompt version.
Validate the signal: check whether evaluator coverage, label delay, or dropped scores changed before concluding that quality moved.
Reproduce the behavior: replay the preserved query against the pinned corpus snapshot.

variants.hint: An evaluation pipeline can move a score by dropping cases, not by answering worse.
variants.explanation: Automated evaluators fail silently, so missing scores and label delay are ruled out before a quality decline is treated as real.

variants.title: Climb the evidence ladder
variants.context: The evidence ladder runs from signal to slice to trace: validate the signal, compare bounded slices, inspect representative traces, reproduce the behavior, then record the attribution. A fleet average says something moved; the slice and the trace say where and how.
variants.prompt: End-to-end p95 latency doubles while availability stays green. Put the investigation in order.

items.text: Record the attribution: link the alert, the divergent span, the owner, and the follow-up evaluation.
Inspect representative traces: compare a slow trace with a fast peer and find the first span that grew, whether provider, retrieval, tool, or retry.
Reproduce the behavior: replay the same request shape against controlled dependencies.
Compare bounded slices: split by model route, region, deployment, and status to find the affected population.
Validate the signal: confirm the latency definition, whether time to first output or end-to-end moved, and the trace sampling policy.

variants.hint: Which span grew is a different question from which service is unhealthy.
variants.explanation: A latency increase can come from a provider, retrieval, a tool, a retry loop, or a longer output, so the first divergent span is what identifies the cause.

variants.title: Build the alert packet
variants.context: A useful alert is a decision packet, not a red number. It names the boundary, proves persistence, attaches the affected population, links the evidence, and declares the owner and response.
variants.prompt: A safety condition on a high-risk tenant class needs an alert. Put the packet in order.

items.text: Link the evidence: attach representative trace IDs, version changes, evaluator results, dependency status, and the last known-good comparison.
Declare the response: name the owner, runbook, rollback target, exposure cap, escalation path, and the condition that resolves the alert.
Name the boundary: define the safety condition before observing the result.
Measure persistence: require a sample count, window, confidence bound, or repeated occurrence so one noisy point does not page anyone.
Attach the population: include the affected feature, route, tenant class, language, risk tier, and exposure.

variants.hint: The boundary has to exist before the number does.
variants.explanation: An alert is useful only when it identifies the affected population, links to reproducible evidence, and names an owned action.

variants.title: Build the alert packet
variants.context: A useful alert is a decision packet, not a red number. It names the boundary, proves persistence, attaches the affected population, links the evidence, and declares the owner and response.
variants.prompt: A team wants to be paged when a feature burns its daily token budget too quickly. Put the packet in order.

items.text: Measure persistence: require the burn to hold across a defined window rather than a single spiky minute.
Attach the population: identify which feature, route, and tenant class is consuming the budget.
Name the boundary: set the cost budget and burn rate that count as a breach.
Declare the response: name the owner, the rate limit or feature disable to apply, the exposure cap, and the resolve condition.
Link the evidence: attach the expensive traces, the prompt and route versions, and the last known-good cost per successful task.

variants.hint: A budget alert without a containment action is a dashboard signal.
variants.explanation: Fast budget exhaustion earns a page only when a tested containment action exists; otherwise it is an investigation or a dashboard signal.

variants.title: Build the alert packet
variants.context: A useful alert is a decision packet, not a red number. It names the boundary, proves persistence, attaches the affected population, links the evidence, and declares the owner and response.
variants.prompt: A quality floor on citation support needs to become an actionable alert. Put the packet in order.

items.text: Attach the population: state which intent, language, and risk tier fell below the floor and how much traffic that is.
Name the boundary: declare the citation-support floor before reading the current score.
Link the evidence: attach sampled evaluator results, reviewer labels, prompt and corpus versions, and matching traces.
Measure persistence: require enough sampled evaluations and a confidence bound before the floor counts as breached.
Declare the response: name the owner, the runbook, the rollback target, the exposure cap, and what closes the alert.

variants.hint: Sparse evidence changes the response, so it belongs in the packet.
variants.explanation: Predeclaring the floor keeps the threshold from being fitted to the result, and the linked evidence is what lets a responder act without an empty dashboard.

variants.title: Operate the monitoring system
variants.context: The monitoring system has its own operating loop: gates and version records on every behavior-changing release, coverage and threshold review on a cadence, and evidence preservation plus after-action review once an incident ends.
variants.prompt: A behavior-changing prompt and retrieval release is about to ship. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Verify alert routing, rollback or feature-disable controls, and trace-to-evaluation joins.
Record model, prompt, retrieval, tool, policy, route, and evaluator versions.
Start with bounded exposure and preserve the release assignment on every trace.
Run predeclared quality, safety, cost, and latency gates against a known-good baseline.

variants.hint: You cannot roll back to a version you never recorded.
variants.explanation: Version records come first because every gate, alert, and rollback target is expressed in terms of them.

variants.title: Operate the monitoring system
variants.context: The monitoring system has its own operating loop: gates and version records on every behavior-changing release, coverage and threshold review on a cadence, and evidence preservation plus after-action review once an incident ends.
variants.prompt: The team runs its periodic monitoring review. Put the cadence steps in order.

items.text: Revisit thresholds after traffic, pricing, architecture, or product objectives change, preserving the prior decision record.
Turn confirmed incidents and near misses into regression cases and runbook tests.
Review signal coverage, missing spans, dropped telemetry, exporter health, evaluator errors, and label delay.
Compare aggregate and critical-slice behavior with denominators and uncertainty.

variants.hint: Check whether the instruments still work before reading them.
variants.explanation: Coverage is reviewed first because missing spans and dropped scores can make a broken slice look healthy in every later comparison.

variants.title: Operate the monitoring system
variants.context: The monitoring system has its own operating loop: gates and version records on every behavior-changing release, coverage and threshold review on a cadence, and evidence preservation plus after-action review once an incident ends.
variants.prompt: An incident is contained and traffic is about to be restored. Put the closing steps in order.

items.text: Document detection delay, exposure, containment, recovery, user impact, and evidence gaps.
Preserve representative traces and the exact version identities that produced the behavior.
Run an after-action review and update monitoring, evaluation, and response controls.
Verify the mitigation against a bounded canary before restoring traffic.

variants.hint: Evidence disappears fastest right after the fix.
variants.explanation: Traces and version identities are preserved first because the mitigation and the after-action review both depend on evidence that expires.

variants.title: Choose the bounded response
variants.context: Quality, cost, and latency guardrails stay independent, and the response is the least disruptive action that still controls exposure: continue the canary, route or disable a feature, roll back, or cap exposure and escalate evaluation.
variants.prompt: A release-attributable groundedness breach is reproduced on the canary, and a known-good version is still deployable. What is the right response?
options: Disable the feature for every tenant until the prompt can be rewritten.
Roll back to the known-good target, since the breach is reproduced and attributable.
Keep the canary running while more evaluator labels are collected for the slice.
optionFeedback: A full feature disable removes healthy behavior when a rollback would restore it.
Correct: a reproduced, release-attributable breach with a known-good target is exactly the rollback case.
Collecting labels is the response to sparse evidence, not to a breach that is already reproduced.
variants.hint: What do you have that a sparse-evidence case does not?
variants.explanation: Roll back when a release-attributable quality or latency breach is reproduced and a known-good target exists; use lighter actions when it is not.

variants.title: Choose the bounded response
variants.context: Quality, cost, and latency guardrails stay independent, and the response is the least disruptive action that still controls exposure: continue the canary, route or disable a feature, roll back, or cap exposure and escalate evaluation.
variants.prompt: Cost per successful task doubles on one optional summarization feature. Quality and safety guardrails pass, and rollback would also remove unrelated healthy behavior. What is the right response?
options: Route, rate-limit, or disable that optional feature while the cost is attributed.
Roll back the whole release, because a hard cost limit was breached.
Accept the cost, because the quality and safety guardrails both pass.
optionFeedback: Correct: an isolated breach where rollback would remove healthy behavior is contained at the feature instead.
Rolling back removes behavior that is not implicated, which is more disruption than the breach requires.
Guardrails are independent, so passing quality does not cancel a breached cost budget.
variants.hint: Which action removes the least healthy behavior while still capping exposure?
variants.explanation: Choose the least disruptive response that controls exposure; a strong result on one guardrail never cancels a breach on another.

variants.title: Choose the bounded response
variants.context: Quality, cost, and latency guardrails stay independent, and the response is the least disruptive action that still controls exposure: continue the canary, route or disable a feature, roll back, or cap exposure and escalate evaluation.
variants.prompt: The mitigation is verified and the incident is contained, but some users received incorrect answers during the window. What has to happen before closing?
options: Close the incident and open a separate ticket for the affected users later.
Reconcile the user-visible effects and preserve the trace before the incident is closed.
Close the incident, since the mitigation is verified and exposure has stopped.
optionFeedback: Deferring reconciliation loses the trace evidence that identifies who was affected.
Correct: user-visible effects are reconciled and the trace preserved before an incident is closed.
Stopping exposure ends the breach, not the obligation to the users already affected.
variants.hint: Containment stops new harm; what about the harm already delivered?
variants.explanation: Closing an incident includes reconciling what users actually received and preserving the trace that proves who was affected.

variants.title: Place the signal
variants.context: Signals belong in different places. Bounded dimensions go on metrics, unbounded identifiers go on traces or controlled event records, raw content stays opt-in, and the response itself goes in a decision record.
variants.prompt: Match each monitoring layer to what it measures.

pairs.label: Service health
pairs.detail: Availability, typed errors, queue delay, rate limits, time to first output, latency, and dependency saturation.

pairs.label: Execution path
pairs.detail: Model calls, retrieval, reranking, policy checks, tool use, retries, fallbacks, and the versions that shaped the result.

pairs.label: Economics
pairs.detail: Input, output, cached, and reasoning tokens plus provider charges attributed to features, routes, tenants, and successful outcomes.

pairs.label: Response behavior
pairs.detail: Groundedness, task success, policy violations, refusals, citation support, evaluator disagreement, and human feedback by slice.

pairs.label: Product outcome
pairs.detail: Whether the user completed the task, retried, abandoned, escalated, corrected the answer, or accepted an unsafe recommendation.

variants.hint: Each layer can fail while the one above it stays green.
variants.explanation: Infrastructure, orchestration, model behavior, and user outcomes fail independently, which is why no single signal describes GenAI health.

variants.title: Place the signal
variants.context: Signals belong in different places. Bounded dimensions go on metrics, unbounded identifiers go on traces or controlled event records, raw content stays opt-in, and the response itself goes in a decision record.
variants.prompt: Match each piece of telemetry to where it belongs.

pairs.label: Service, deployment, model route, region, and status
pairs.detail: Low-cardinality metrics used for fleet trends and paging.

pairs.label: Request IDs, prompt versions, document IDs, and tool arguments
pairs.detail: Traces or controlled event records, joined back by stable IDs during investigation.

pairs.label: Raw prompts, outputs, and retrieved text
pairs.detail: Opt-in collection with a declared purpose, redaction, access control, and short retention.

pairs.label: Threshold, affected slice, owner, mitigation, and rollback target
pairs.detail: The decision record that preserves how the response was chosen.

variants.hint: Ask whether the field is bounded, unbounded, sensitive, or a decision.
variants.explanation: Unbounded identifiers on metrics create runaway series, and raw content turns a telemetry pipeline into a sensitive data store.

variants.title: Place the signal
variants.context: Signals belong in different places. Bounded dimensions go on metrics, unbounded identifiers go on traces or controlled event records, raw content stays opt-in, and the response itself goes in a decision record.
variants.prompt: Match each situation to the alert class it earns.

pairs.label: A confirmed severe safety event with a tested containment action
A statistically credible quality regression that needs attribution but not a shutdown
Material possible impact where production evidence is sparse, delayed, or contested between evaluators
An informative change with no predeclared response and no owner
pairs.detail: Keep it as a dashboard signal.

variants.hint: The class follows from the evidence and the owned action, not from how alarming the number looks.
variants.explanation: Matching the alert to the failure keeps pages meaningful; a change with no predeclared response and no owner is not an alert at all.
